people.summary: Named on the back of a beach snapshot as the father of Reg and Bob, and seen there in a clerical collar. A Knightsbridge cabinet card probably shows him too. The family links him to the Earls of Orkney as a son of Henry Warrender FitzMaurice; the records dispute it.
people.story:
A snapshot in the family collection shows a man in a clerical collar and a boater, sitting on a shingle beach with two small boys. The label on the back reads "Reg, Bob and their Father Edward Dixon Fitzmaurice".[^photo-labels][^beach-snapshots] It is the only record in the collection that names him.

A cabinet card by the Stuart studio at 47 and 49 Brompton Road, Knightsbridge, shows a clergyman in round wire spectacles. It carries no name, but the face matches the man on the beach, and it is taken here to be Edward Dixon. The 2026 photo analysis dated the card's style to about 1890 to 1910.[^stuart-card][^genealogy-report]

## The Orkney question

Earlier versions of this site said Edward Dixon was almost certainly a son of the Hon. Henry Warrender FitzMaurice. That would make him a brother of the 7th Earl of Orkney and would connect this family to the Earls of Orkney, the Dukes of Hamilton and King James II of Scotland.[^site-earlier]

The records found for this revision do not support it. Henry Warrender married Sarah Jane Roose in 1861, and the peerage lists their children as Henry George Hamilton, Edmond Walter, Isabella Emily and Alexander.[^peerage-henry-warrender] In April 1890 a royal warrant printed in the London Gazette gave the rank of an earl's children to the brother and sister of the new 7th Earl. It names only two, Alexander Edmond Fitzmaurice and Isabella Emily Garrett.[^gazette-1890] Any older legitimate son would have inherited the earldom himself. The 2026 photo analysis dated the beach snapshot to about 1905 to 1920 from its format and the clothing, so Edward Dixon was almost certainly alive in 1890 too.[^genealogy-report] If he had been a legitimate son of Henry Warrender, he would have been named in the warrant, and if he was older than Edmond he would have inherited the earldom himself in 1889. He was therefore not a legitimate son of Henry Warrender.

That does not rule out some other connection to the wider FitzMaurice family, but none has been found. This tree still draws the line from Henry Warrender to Edward Dixon, as the family has always told it, so that the Orkney relationships can be followed. The line is dashed and marked as disputed, and every relationship that runs through it says so.

## Still to find

His birth, ordination and parishes should appear in Crockford's Clerical Directory and in the censuses from 1881 to 1911. Earlier pages gave his birth as about 1850, and the handoff brief as about 1843, both without a source. The 2026 photo analysis put his age in the cabinet card at about 30 to 45.[^site-earlier][^handoff-brief][^genealogy-report]

people.story:
A small circular portrait of a young woman in a pale gown, holding flowers, is inscribed on the back "Edith Madeleine Fitzmaurice c.1899".[^edith-medallion] The "c." suggests the date was written later by someone estimating it. The 2026 photo analysis put her age in the portrait at late teens to mid-twenties and the dress at about 1895 to 1905.[^genealogy-report]

How Edith fits the family is not known. Earlier pages call her Reg's sister and Edward Dixon's daughter, but nothing in the collection says so, and the photo analysis suggested she might instead be Edward Dixon's sister.[^site-earlier][^genealogy-report] Reg's own children are not involved: Amanda names Reg, Bob and Babs, and does not mention Edith.[^family-account] She is shown here beside Edward Dixon, in a frame marked "relationship unproven".

A faded full-length cabinet card from the Lang Sims studio, of 437 Brixton Road and 9 Church Street, Folkestone, shows a woman who looks similar, with the same pinned-up hair and a bouquet. It may be her, but it is unlabelled.[^lang-sims-card][^genealogy-report]

people.story:
The oldest photograph in the collection is a carte de visite of a seated woman in a dark, full-skirted dress, with a young girl standing beside a small table. The back carries the printed stamp of J. Perriman, Camden Town School of Photography, 3 Greenland Place, "Side of the Mother Red Cap", with the number 925 written in.[^perriman-cdv] The 2026 photo analysis dated the dress and format to about 1865 to 1878.[^genealogy-report]

Neither sitter is named. Earlier pages call them unknown FitzMaurice ancestors. That is a reasonable guess from where the card was kept, but nothing on it says so, and they could belong to any branch of the family.[^site-earlier] They are shown here as a single card in the "relationship unproven" frame.

people.story:
Reg FitzMaurice was Patricia's father. The wedding album of February 1950 names him as Mr R. Fitzmaurice of Hayes, Middlesex. Its captions say Pat was "given away by her father", and a guest labelled "Father" stands on the church steps in both group photographs.[^album-1950] His granddaughter Amanda confirms that Reg was her grandfather and Bob his brother.[^family-account]

A snapshot of a clergyman with two small boys on a shingle beach is labelled on the back "Reg, Bob and their Father Edward Dixon Fitzmaurice".[^photo-labels][^beach-snapshots] The label does not say which boy is which, or when it was written. That this Reg is Pat's father is the family's reading, and it fits the initial R. in the album, so his link to Edward Dixon is shown as probable rather than proven.

His wife, Pat's mother, had died by February 1950.[^album-1950] Family tradition says Reg himself later died of an illness linked to smoking.[^family-account] His date of birth is not known. Earlier versions of this site gave about 1897, with no source.[^site-earlier]

A studio portrait of a young man in a bow tie is captioned as Reg on earlier pages. The photograph is unlabelled, and the handoff brief describes the same image as unidentified, so it is shown here as a possible portrait only.[^young-man-portrait][^handoff-brief]

people.summary: Known to the family as Auntie Babs. A snapshot of a girl on a verandah is labelled "Auntie Babs, South Africa". Shown as Reg's sister, which is the family's reading.
people.story:
Babs is remembered in the family as Auntie Babs. A snapshot of a girl in a white dress and dark tie, standing on a verandah beside a palm, is labelled on the back "Auntie Babs / South Africa". On the front, at the edge, are the letters "Eil", which may be the start of her real first name.[^photo-labels][^beach-snapshots]

Amanda calls her "my auntie", and earlier pages place her as Reg's sister.[^family-account][^site-earlier] Families often called a great-aunt "auntie", so she is shown here as Reg's sister, marked probable. Her full name is the key to finding her in any record.

A guest labelled "Auntie Babs" stands on the church steps in both group photographs at Pat and Ron's wedding in 1950.[^album-1950] She is probably the same woman, which would mean she was in England that February, but the album does not say. Another snapshot in the collection shows a single-storey house with a verandah in a garden. Earlier pages link it to her life in South Africa, but it is unlabelled.[^sa-snapshots][^site-earlier]

people.summary: Ronald's father. Only his initials survive, in the 1950 wedding album. Family tradition says he was killed with his wife and youngest son when their East Ham home was bombed.
people.story:
Ron's father is known from one line in the wedding album of February 1950, which calls Ron the son of "the late Mr. and Mrs. H. G. Andrews, of East Ham, London". Only his initials are recorded.[^album-1950]

Family tradition says he, his wife and their youngest son were killed when their home in East Ham was bombed during the Second World War.[^family-account][^site-earlier] The Blitz on London began on 7 September 1940 with raids on the docks of east London, and East Ham lay beside them.[^ctx-blitz] The date of the bombing that killed the family is not known.

Earlier pages identify him as the man in the flat cap in the Andrews family photograph. One caption on the earlier tree also names him Sidney, which does not fit the initials H. G.[^site-earlier][^andrews-family-photo]

people.story:
Ronald Andrews was the son of "the late Mr. and Mrs. H. G. Andrews, of East Ham, London", as his wedding album records.[^album-1950] Family tradition says his parents and his younger brother were killed when their East Ham home was bombed during the war, and that his brother Herbert survived.[^family-account][^site-earlier]

## Egypt

Ron kept an album of his time in Egypt and captioned it in his own hand. A press card pasted into it certifies "L.A.C. R. Andrews" as Art Editor of the "Tura Times", the newspaper of 111 M.U., R.A.F., so he was a Leading Aircraftman with No. 111 Maintenance Unit.[^ron-album] The unit was formed in August 1941 and worked in limestone caves at Tura, south of Cairo, repairing aircraft engines. The caves had been quarried in ancient times for the casing stones of the pyramids.[^wiki-raf-tura] In one photograph his overalls are marked "3ERS". RAF Tura also housed a No. 3 Engine Repair Section, so that is probably what the letters mean.[^ron-workshop][^wiki-raf-tura]

His captions describe the work: a 2,200 horsepower "Double Wasp" radial on assembly, a "Twin Wasp" crankshaft measured with a micrometer "to within 1/10,000!", and the smallest and largest engines in the shop. Photography was not allowed inside, and he wrote that his friend Johnie "smuggled his Leica into the caves 'Security Area' and took these shots of our worktime".[^ron-album]

In his spare time he drew, copying portraits of film stars: "Re-kindled the urge to draw ... but in the copying work ... this time Deanna Durbin". A drawing of Betty Hutton is labelled "Photo of a drawing of a photo". He bought his first camera from Bert Spencer and photographed Cairo, including the Anglican Cathedral and the Opera Cinema at night. Under one picture he wrote "This won Johnnie a prize in Cairo exhibition", and under the next, "... and this didn't".[^ron-album]

On one page he wrote that the treasures of Tutankhamun "were stored in our caves during the War and later placed on view in the Museum. They were worth the journey to see." No other record in this collection confirms that the treasures were kept at Tura.[^ron-album] The album also keeps a copy of the Tura Times "First Peace Edition", headed "Peace after nearly six years".[^ron-album]

One caption mentions a comrade called Reg who was ill "on the Boat" and later died of a duodenal ulcer. He is not Reg FitzMaurice, Pat's father.[^ron-album][^family-account]

## Pat

Ron and Pat were introduced by friends, the parents of Sandra, and married at St Mary's Church, Wanstead, on 11 February 1950. His best man was Laurie.[^family-account][^album-1950] Forty years later the family held a ruby wedding dinner for them at The French Horn in Sonning.[^ruby-invitation] Ron has since died.[^family-account]

people.summary: Daughter of Reg FitzMaurice of Hayes and of a mother who died young. Born in Windsor and evacuated in the war, she married Ronald Andrews at St Mary's, Wanstead, on 11 February 1950.
people.story:
Patricia Mary FitzMaurice married Ronald Andrews at St Mary's Church, Wanstead, at half past ten on the morning of Saturday 11 February 1950. The wedding album names her as the daughter of "Mr. and the late Mrs. R. Fitzmaurice, of Hayes, Middlesex", so her mother had died before the wedding.[^album-1950] The family identifies her father as Reg FitzMaurice.[^family-account]

## Before the wedding

Family tradition says Pat was born in Windsor, that her mother died while she was still young, and that she was evacuated to the English countryside during the Second World War.[^family-account] Where she was sent, and how old she was, is not recorded. The government's evacuation scheme, Operation Pied Piper, began on 1 September 1939.[^ctx-pied-piper] Her date of birth and her mother's name are still to be found.

She and Ron were introduced by friends, the parents of Sandra. A Sandra is named among the guests in both wedding group photographs.[^family-account][^album-1950]

## The wedding day

The service was taken by the Reverend A. E. Gates. The album explains that guests had come "from various far-away places", leaving little time for photographs before the service, so its first picture shows the couple walking down the aisle as "Mr. and Mrs. Ronald Andrews". Pat was given away by her father. She wore a navy-blue suit, a dusty-pink halo hat, grey suede shoes and gloves, and carried a grey suede bag, with a spray of red roses at her shoulder.[^album-1950]

The reception was held at the Wanstead home of Mr and Mrs Jack Winter. One caption reads: "Jack took over the man's job of feeding the multitude. June wonders if that big slice is for her, while Pat thinks perhaps there should be a catering licence." The toast was drunk in sherry. To leave, Pat wore a grey whip-cord overcoat with a hat of pillar-box red, and the couple left for Waterloo and a honeymoon in Bournemouth.[^album-1950]

## Later

Forty years on, the family held a ruby wedding dinner for Pat and Ron at The French Horn in Sonning. The invitation gives the date as Saturday 10 March, which fits 1990.[^ruby-invitation] Amanda and Venetia are their daughters.[^family-account] Pat has since died. The box of photographs that started this site was laid out on a table after her service.[^family-account][^site-earlier]

people.summary: King of Scots from the age of six, after the murder of his father in 1437. He was killed when one of his own cannon exploded at the siege of Roxburgh in 1460.
people.story:
James II became King of Scots in 1437, at the age of six, after his father James I was murdered. He was known as "Fiery Face" for a red birthmark on one side of his face.[^wiki-james-ii]

He married Mary of Guelders in 1449. In August 1460 he was besieging Roxburgh Castle, then held by the English, when one of his cannon exploded beside him and killed him. He was 29.[^wiki-james-ii]

His daughter Mary Stewart married into the Hamilton family, and through her the Hamiltons came close to the Scottish throne.[^wiki-mary-stewart]

## Link to this family

The family traces Sebastian's line to this person through Edward Dixon FitzMaurice, as a son of Henry Warrender FitzMaurice. That step is not proven, and the 1890 London Gazette record speaks against it (see Edward Dixon FitzMaurice). On 25 November 1695 he married Elizabeth Villiers, and on 3 January 1696 he was made Earl of Orkney.[^wiki-george-orkney] He bought Cliveden in Buckinghamshire and lived there and at Taplow.[^wiki-george-orkney] He was appointed Governor of Virginia but never went there. In 1736 he became the first officer in the British Army to hold the rank of Field Marshal, and he died in January 1737.[^wiki-george-orkney]

He had daughters but no son. The earldom could pass to a daughter, and his eldest, Anne, became the 2nd Countess.[^wiki-george-orkney][^wiki-anne-countess]

On 19 July 1892 he married Connie Gilchrist, a former child performer of the Gaiety Theatre.[^wiki-connie] The Evening News of 1951 describes him as of The Tythe House, Stewkley, near Leighton Buzzard, a Deputy Lieutenant for Buckinghamshire and a former Master of the Whaddon Chase Foxhounds.[^korea-clipping]

Their only child, Lady Mary Constance Hamilton FitzMaurice, was born in 1903. She married, had no children, and died in October 1950, ten months before her father.[^peerage-henry-warrender][^wiki-connie] When Edmond died in August 1951 he left the residue of his estate of £42,893 to Cecil FitzMaurice, who also inherited the earldom. The paper called Edmond Cecil's great-uncle; by the peerage records he was Cecil's first cousin twice removed.[^korea-clipping][^press-1951][^peerage-cecil]

Earlier pages give his name as "Edmond Walter Leighton FitzMaurice" and say he inherited at 16. "Leighton" comes from the Leighton Buzzard address, and he was 22.[^site-earlier][^korea-clipping]

people.story:
Connie Gilchrist was born in January 1865. As a child she modelled for painters: Whistler painted her as "The Gold Girl", posed as she appeared on the Gaiety Theatre stage in her skipping-rope dance, and she was the girl in Frederic Leighton's "The Music Lesson".[^wiki-connie][^met-gold-girl] She performed at the Gaiety and became known as "the original Gaiety Girl".[^wiki-connie]

She had left the stage by July 1892, when she married Edmond FitzMaurice, 7th Earl of Orkney.[^wiki-connie] They were married for 54 years. She died in May 1946.[^wiki-connie][^korea-clipping] The 1951 newspaper report gives her age at death as 73; from her date of birth she was 81.[^korea-clipping][^wiki-connie]

people.story:
Cecil O'Bryen FitzMaurice was the younger son of Douglas Frederick Harold FitzMaurice and Dorothy Dickie. He joined the Royal Army Service Corps in 1939 and served in North Africa, Italy, France and Germany, and then in Korea.[^wiki-cecil][^peerage-cecil]

He became the 8th Earl of Orkney on 21 August 1951 while serving as a driver in Korea. Newspapers called him "the Earl from Korea".[^press-1951][^korea-clipping] The Evening News reported that his Army friends knew him as "Ginger", that the 7th Earl had left him the residue of an estate of £42,893, and that on the voyage home he was given four days' confinement to barracks and set to scrub the mess decks for coming back late to the ship at Colombo.[^korea-clipping] The paper called the 7th Earl his great-uncle; he was in fact a much more distant cousin.[^korea-clipping][^peerage-cecil]

On 27 November 1953 he married Rose Katherine Durk Silley at St Mary's, Brixham. The Evening News said she helped her mother run a 60-bedroom hotel in the town, and that the Earl had once worked in a garage.[^marries-clipping][^peerage-cecil] Rose died in 1995. Cecil died in February 1998 with no children, and the earldom passed to a distant cousin, Peter St John.[^wiki-cecil][^wiki-earl-of-orkney]

Earlier pages give the year of his marriage as 1952. The peerage records give 1953.[^site-earlier][^peerage-cecil]
